messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus Chen was thirty-six when he came to therapy, though his wife Sarah said he had seemed much older since he returned from his second deployment in 2019. He had spent fourteen months in Kandahar province as a logistics officer, managing supply chains and coordinating with local contractors. On a Tuesday in March of that year, during what should have been a routine site inspection at a forward operating base, an IED detonated near the convoy. Marcus was thrown from the vehicle. Two soldiers died. He sustained a fractured collarbone and severe lacerations but walked away conscious and mobile—a fact that had come to feel, in his mind, like a debt he could never repay.

The first weeks after the explosion passed in a blur of medical evaluations and debriefing. Marcus returned stateside in June. By autumn, Sarah noticed he had stopped inviting friends over, that he flinched when she reached for his hand in bed, that he would sit rigid at the dinner table if there was any lull in conversation. She attributed it to readjustment. Marcus told himself the same thing. But the truth was more intricate: he had come to believe that the world operated on a logic of sudden violence, that safety was an illusion maintained only through constant vigilance. Silence, in particular, had become intolerable. In quiet moments—the pause before a colleague spoke in a meeting, the gap between songs on the radio, his wife's thoughtful silence while reading—Marcus felt the air thicken with menace, as if danger was coalescing in the emptiness. He had learned to fill those spaces with sound, with movement, with anything that kept the world knowable.

By early 2020, his avoidance had calcified into patterns that structured his days. He would not allow Sarah to touch him—not a hand on his shoulder, not an embrace, nothing. When she tried, his body seized with alarm, his nervous system interpreting her touch as a threat that required immediate escape. He had stopped talking with her about the deployment entirely; the few times she had gently asked how he was really doing, he had felt something like nausea rise in his throat, a sense that speaking about it would make it real in a way that might destroy him. He had begun, without fully recognizing it, to push away moments of contentment. When Sarah would laugh at something on television, or when he found himself briefly absorbed in a task at work, he would feel a cold dread: this peace was false, he thought. Letting himself feel safe was a betrayal of the men who had died, and it was dangerous—a lowering of the guard that would make him vulnerable.

His work as a tax consultant had become a minefield. Confrontations with clients over deductions or audit findings triggered a surge of hyperarousal that left him shaking. Certain conversation topics—anything involving explosions, accidents, sudden loss—would send him spiraling. And he had developed an elaborate system of identifying exits in every office building he entered, every conference room, every restaurant where he met a client. He could not feel settled until he knew the way out.

The memories themselves came in two distinct forms, neither of which felt fully his own. Sometimes he would taste copper and burnt plastic, the sensations so vivid and intrusive that they would derail his afternoon, leaving him unable to concentrate. Other times, he could recall the sequence of events with perfect clarity—the sound, the impact, the smell of smoke—but feel absolutely nothing, as if he were watching a film about someone else's trauma. Most destabilizing were the moments when emotion flooded in: the memory would return in full sensory detail, and the grief and terror would be so overwhelming that he would have to excuse himself from meetings, lock himself in the bathroom, wait for the wave to pass.

By November of last year, Sarah had stopped trying to touch him. She had stopped asking him to talk. She had begun sleeping in the guest room. It was this—the quiet dissolution of his marriage, the realization that his protective mechanisms were destroying the one relationship that might have anchored him—that finally brought Marcus to seek help. He sat in the first session with his shoulders braced, as if expecting impact, and said only this: "I'm losing her, and I don't know how to stop it."
